entities.name: Annibale Annibaldi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Annibale Annibaldi (died 1272) was a preeminent Italian Catholic theologian, Dominican friar, and cardinal whose intellectual contributions significantly shaped scholastic thought and papal policy during the High Middle Ages. A key figure in the Dominican Order's intellectual ascendancy, he served as a trusted advisor to several popes, most notably Urban IV, and played a crucial role in defending the mendicant orders against secular attacks, thereby influencing the theological and institutional landscape of the 13th century Church. His career spanned a period of intense intellectual ferment and ecclesiastical consolidation, making him a bridge between academic theology and practical Church governance in the Papal States.

Born into the powerful Annibaldi family of Rome, Annibale's early education and entry into the Dominican Order are not precisely documented, but he rose to prominence as a master of theology at the University of Paris, a crucible of scholastic thought, by 1256. During his tenure, he was a vocal defender of the mendicant orders against the criticisms of secular masters like William of Saint-Amour, whose polemics challenged the friars' right to teach and preach. His scholarly acumen and loyalty to the papacy led to his elevation as Cardinal-Priest of Santi XII Apostoli by Pope Urban IV in 1262, after which he served as a papal legate and advisor, contributing to the formulation of ecclesiastical doctrine and policy. He was deeply involved in the intellectual currents of his time, interacting with luminaries such as Thomas Aquinas, and his writings reflect a sophisticated engagement with Aristotelian philosophy and Christian theology.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Annibale Annibaldi's role as a leading Dominican theologian and cardinal helped solidify the intellectual and institutional standing of mendicant orders, influencing subsequent Church structure and theological development. His work contributed to the broader acceptance of Aristotelian philosophy within Christian thought, impacting the intellectual trajectory of the 13th century.
